recordings.text: Nice and simple, really: one piece settles on a square that reaches several targets, and a single reply is unlikely to look after all of them.
Here's the plain fact about this move: one of the other side's pieces now has a square where it can fork several targets. Find that piece and the square, and the pattern is clear.
The stronger move had a fork tucked inside it, one piece reaching for several targets together. Worth setting it up afterward and playing it through calmly.
The pinned piece is stuck in front of its own king now, and a sturdy pin it is. If it stepped off the line, its own king would be in check.
The plain issue is a pin: after this move, a piece standing in front of its king can be pinned there and won't be allowed to step aside.
The stronger move would have frozen an enemy piece in front of its king. This one lets that piece wander freely, and that's the whole difference.
A neat skewer. The front piece has to step out of the way, and then whatever was hiding behind it can be collected.
Simply put: two pieces end up on one line where the other side can skewer them, front one forced aside, back one left to be picked up.
The stronger move had a skewer to offer: lean on the front piece, collect the one behind. A good pattern to keep handy.
The defender is captured, and whatever it was looking after is left on its own. Straightforward and effective.
Here's the plain risk: one defender could be captured now, and the piece it protects would be left without that help.
The stronger move took out a defender and left the piece behind it unprotected. It's a useful idea to keep handy.
The weak spot is the back rank, plain and simple. The king's own pieces are sitting where it would want to escape, so that last rank is open to attack.
The point to see is the back rank: after this move the king has no way off it, and the other side can mate along that rank.
The enemy king was stuck on its back rank behind its own pieces, and a mate was there. Worth replaying slowly to see how it would have gone.
The pawn takes another step toward promotion. Count what's left in the race; the defense has fewer moves to stop it now.
The plain fact is that an enemy pawn now has a clearer road to promotion. Every step it takes from here will want an answer.
The stronger move kept a pawn rolling toward promotion. Here it stays put, and the race looks different because of that.
The piece in front moves aside, and suddenly the one behind it is attacking down the line. Tidy little idea.
Something to settle and look at: one enemy piece is hiding another, and when the front one moves, the back one attacks along the line.
Tucked into the stronger move was a discovered attack, one piece stepping aside so the piece behind could strike. That line stayed closed here.
One move, two threats, nice and simple. A single reply rarely manages both.
The plain problem: after this move, the other side has a single move that makes two threats at once.
Two threats would have come from the stronger move together. This one doesn't make that pair, and that's the gap.
The defender is tempted away from its post, and what it was covering is left open. Neat and practical.
The simple risk here is a deflection: one defender can be pulled off the piece or square it's covering.
The stronger move pulled a defender away from its job. Set it up afterward and see what falls apart once that defender leaves.
That piece was sitting there unguarded, so it's taken without any cost. Checking for loose pieces like that is a good habit.
An unguarded enemy piece was there to collect with the stronger move. A quick scan for loose pieces before a quiet move catches these.
The plain issue here: one piece is left with nothing guarding it, and the other side can simply pick it up.
The simple problem is that this piece was the only real guard of another one. Once it moves away, that other piece can be captured.
A threat came with the opponent's last move, and this reply doesn't deal with it. That leaves a piece open to capture.
Play the trade out one more move. The recapture wins back more than was taken, so the exchange ends up costing material.
One more minor piece is out of its starting square and part of the game now. Steady, sensible development.
With another move, a minor piece would have been out and working. Here it's still at home.

Another move would have given a rook a pawnless file, top to bottom.

Another move would have handed a rook a semi-open file, free of its own pawns with enemy pawns up ahead.
That pawn has become a passed pawn. With no enemy pawn in front of it on its file or the ones next door, there's no pawn that can stop it.
With another move, a pawn would have become passed, with nothing of the enemy's to stop it on its file or either side.
The passed pawn rolls one square further. Count how many are left, and keep an eye on who can still stop it.
